title: Is Wonder the dinner company for our anti-social times? | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Dinnertime in America once looked like a family gathering around the table to eat mom’s cooking. Then came restaurants, fast food and takeout.

Now, when people still do get together for dinner, food delivery company Wonder wants them to eat their own personal portions of Thai, Japanese and Mediterranean.

Wonder represents the extreme crackup of sharing a meal in America. The companyoffers more than two dozen types of cuisines —some from recognizable restaurant names and celebrity chefs — cooked out of roughly 170 storefronts it has opened in the Northeast in three years. Wonder has also bought Grubhub and Blue Apron, and it lists its individual brands like Limesalt on delivery apps.

Wonder promises a kind of food abundance for families and friends struggling to agree on what to order for dinner: “the destination for every craving without compromise.”

But ordering Chinese with friends when you’re in the mood for Mexican is not a problem that needs to be solved. It’s a normal part of being human. By the time you’re passing around dumplings and noodles, you’ll forgot you wanted tacos.

At a moment when many consumers crave authenticity and community in an isolated, tech-fueled world, Wonder is offering steaks with Bobby Flay’s name on them mass prepared offsite and finished in nondescript “food halls” that look like an AI mashup of Sweetgreen and Starbucks. Speedy delivery and sleek branding are what matters above all, Wonder is betting.

Wonder is not about the “community-based, squishy, ephemeral things” associated with food, said Lilly Jan, a chef and assistant teaching professor in the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business. “It’s a fast-fashion model for restaurants.”

Wonder, valued at $9 billion and heading toward anIPO, says it’sbringing high-quality food to the suburbs and less densely-populated parts of the country where some individual restaurants couldn’t survive economically. It also offers lower prices than most delivery apps, zero fees and overnight options.

“We believe a shared meal is about sitting down and spending time together, not about everyone eating the same thing,” a Wonder spokesperson said. “Wonder lets everyone get something they love and still eat together.”

Wonder is the brainchild ofMarc Lore, the master of online shopping. Lore foundedDiapers.comandJet.com.

He started Wonder in 2018 as a so-called ghost kitchen offering different cuisines out of food trucks. The companypivotedto brick-and-mortar storefronts after the pandemic.

Wall Street is high on Lore’s vision and Wonder’s cost-cutting technology. The company has developed a robot that can make about500 bowlsan hour, Lore has said. Investors also see potential inWonder Create, a new program that lets anyone launch a restaurant on Wonder’s platform without paying for rent or labor.

“Restaurants in our world are just software,” Lore said of Wonder Create. “They’re brands, logos and recipes that plug into the platform.”

But many consumers are already fed up with AI-generated food images on menus and in advertising — “AI slop menus,” as some TikTokers have dubbed them. Vandals recently graffitied a San Francisco restaurant that used AI-generated images of bacon, egg and cheese sandwiches.

Any takers for ChatGPT-designed restaurants?

The idea of eating with a group of people at a restaurant with some character still matters to many people. Restaurants are a place to gather, try new foods and explore. They’re connected to a place and make up the fabric of neighborhoods.

Wonder strips away the traditional relationship between restaurant and customer and turns it into a commodity, said Stephen Zagor, a restaurant consultant who teaches at Columbia Business School. That’s why some foodies and locals worried about the future of neighborhood restaurants have been unusually hostile online to Wonder’s arrival.

The 300,000-memberr/FoodNYCsubreddit has become a place for people to gripe about Wonder popping up in their backyard, where there are too many restaurant options to count. Many of the comments go beyond the usual criticism of a restaurant’s food, or puzzlement over why anyone in New York City would order Wonder’s Thai instead of calling the neighborhood Thai joint 10 minutes away.

Wonder says it’s not trying to replace restaurants and takes customer criticism seriously.But some of the pushback online reflects a deeper frustration with the homogenization and automation of American dining, symbolized by the growing presence of Wonder storefronts.

“The thing about Wonder that I keep coming back to is its total lack of a reason to exist,” the writer Laura Aultsaidin a scathing piece about the company in the independent news outlet New Caananite in March. “Save for yet another late-stage capitalism ‘disruption’ plot.”
